title: The Reciprocity of Liking and Team Cohesion
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Drawing on research into the reciprocity of liking, this article argues that the most likable people aren't simply confident or warm, they're the ones who express liking for others first. That liking gets returned, creating a cycle that strengthens relationships even in digital interactions like social media likes. In the workplace specifically, the piece catalogs concrete signals people read as evidence of being liked: genuine compliments, attentive listening, inclusive language, and supportive nonverbals. The author ties this directly to team chemistry, arguing that mutual liking, not just shared identity, is often the missing ingredient in cohesive teams.
points: The most likable people tend to have the longest lists of people they express liking for first
Liking is reciprocal, even in digital interactions like social media likes among strangers
Workplace signals of liking include genuine compliments, inclusive language, and supportive body language
Mutual liking, not just shared identity, is often the real driver of strong team chemistry
quotes: As it turns out, the most likable people have the longest lists of people they like. By expressing liking first, people respond in kind.
Research behind the Reciprocity of Liking proves that people are attracted to and like others who express liking for them.
This reciprocity effect occurs in digital interaction as well. People have a strong tendency to reciprocate “likes” on a social media platform, even with people they don’t know.
Colleagues perceive genuine compliments, positive feedback, attentive listening, making time for small talk, inclusive language (we, our), a willingness to offer assistance
Leaders who encourage more of the behaviors of liking and display them in their own interactions create the most positive workplaces and most cohesive teams.
